notes.meaning: Satan rose up against Israel and pushed David to count the fighting men. Taking a count was not bad by itself, but David did it out of pride to measure his own power rather than trusting in God's promises. God allowed this temptation to test David, showing that even the best leaders must guard against sinful pride.

differ.view: God sovereignly ordained the temptation to punish Israel while remaining entirely free of sin, using Satan as a secondary agent to carry it out.
God did not cause or ordain David's sin, but permitted Satan to accuse and tempt David before the heavenly court.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God merely permitted David to be tempted and to fall into sin, without actively instigating the evil act Himself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Second Samuel explains the event from an older theological perspective where God initiates all things, whereas Chronicles reflects later Jewish thought by attributing the temptation directly to Satan.

notes.meaning: David ordered Joab and his army leaders to count all the soldiers from Beersheba in the south to Dan in the north. He wanted a complete total so he could know the size of his army. The people of Israel belonged to God alone, so David was acting as if they were his own personal possession.

Joab pleaded with David to change his mind. He prayed that the Lord would multiply the soldiers a hundred times over, and reminded the king that all Israelites were already his loyal servants. Joab warned that this needless counting was rooted in pride and would bring guilt and divine judgment upon the whole nation.

David overruled Joab's wise advice and forced the army leaders to carry out the census. Joab obeyed with great reluctance, traveling across the country for nearly ten months before returning to Jerusalem. When leaders ignore godly warnings, their stubbornness can easily put others in harm's way.

Joab reported the final numbers of the army to David. There were 1,100,000 men capable of drawing the sword in Israel, and 470,000 fighting men in Judah. These vast numbers showed how faithfully God had kept His ancient promise to multiply the descendants of Abraham.

Joab left out the tribes of Levi and Benjamin from the official count because he hated the king's order. Levi was already exempt by God's law from military service to care for the sanctuary, and Benjamin was the smallest tribe. Joab was so sickened by the project that he stopped before finishing the work.

God looked upon David's command as wicked, and He struck Israel with judgment. The census displeased the Lord because it was done out of pride and vain curiosity rather than trust in God. This verse summarizes the punishment that was about to unfold across the land.

David's conscience struck him, and he openly confessed his wrongdoing to God. He admitted that he had sinned greatly and acted very foolishly. He begged the Lord to remove his iniquity, which means his guilt and sin, showing a humble desire to make things right with God.

The Lord spoke directly to Gad, who was David's personal seer or prophet. Even though David was a great king and had spiritual gifts of his own, God sent outside messengers to correct him when he went astray. Gad served as God's trusted voice to deliver difficult truth to the king.

God sent Gad to present David with three distinct choices for his punishment. The king had to choose which penalty he would endure, and God promised to carry it out. This forced David to face the severe consequences of his pride and submit to the Lord's discipline.

Gad came before David to deliver the Lord's solemn message. He told the king plainly that he must make a choice between the punishments God offered. There was no escaping the rod of correction once sin had run its course.

The three options were three years of famine, three months of being chased and struck down by enemies, or three days of a deadly plague carried out by the angel of the Lord. Each choice grew shorter in time but far more intense in its danger. Gad urged David to decide quickly so he could take an answer back to the Lord.

David felt deeply distressed by the terrible choices before him. He decided to choose the plague, asking to fall into the hands of the Lord because God's mercies are great and boundless. He refused to fall into human hands, knowing that human enemies show little pity in war.

The Lord sent a deadly plague upon Israel, and seventy thousand men died. David had taken great pride in the huge size of his army, so divine justice cut that number down. It was a terrible demonstration of how one leader's pride can bring sorrow upon thousands.

God sent an angel to destroy Jerusalem, but as the devastation began, the Lord showed mercy and stopped the judgment. He told the angel that it was enough and ordered him to pull back his hand. The angel was standing at that moment by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, just outside the city walls.

David looked up and saw the angel of the Lord suspended between earth and heaven with a drawn sword pointed over Jerusalem. David and the elders wore sackcloth, which were rough, scratchy clothes used to show deep sorrow and repentance, and they fell on their faces. The drawn sword made God's holy anger against sin clearly visible to everyone.

David cried out to God, taking the full blame upon himself for ordering the census. He called the people innocent sheep and asked why they should suffer for his wicked failure. Like a true shepherd, he begged God to punish him and his own family rather than letting the plague destroy the people.

The angel of the Lord told Gad to instruct David to go up and build an altar on Ornan's threshing floor. Building an altar was a sign that God was opening a path of peace and reconciliation. The very angel who had brought judgment now provided the way for God's anger to be turned away.

David obeyed immediately and went up to the hill just as Gad had told him in the name of the Lord. He did not make excuses or delay his journey. Quick obedience is the only proper response when God reveals how to turn away His judgment.

Ornan was busy threshing his wheat when he turned and saw the angel of the Lord. The sight of the heavenly messenger with a drawn sword terrified Ornan's four sons, so they ran and hid. Weak human beings naturally tremble in fear when faced with the holy power of the spiritual realm.

As David approached the threshing floor, Ornan looked up and recognized the king. He immediately came out of his work area and bowed down with his face to the dirt to show honor and respect to David. This meeting between the king and the landowner prepared the way for the altar to be raised.

David asked Ornan to sell him the threshing floor for its full market value so he could build an altar to the Lord. He explained that a sacrifice was needed right away so the plague destroying the nation would stop. Even though David was king, he did not take the land by force, but sought to buy it fairly.

Ornan generously urged the king to take whatever he wanted as a free gift. He offered his oxen for the animal sacrifices, his wooden threshing sledges for firewood, and his wheat for the grain offering. Ornan was eager to give everything he had to help stop the plague and honor God.

David firmly refused the gift and insisted on paying the complete price for the land and supplies. He declared that he would not give God something that belonged to another person, nor would he offer sacrifices that cost him nothing. True worship requires genuine sacrifice from our own hearts and hands.

David paid Ornan six hundred shekels of gold by weight to buy the entire property. While he had bought the oxen and tools for silver, he purchased the whole mountain site with gold. This very plot of land on Mount Moriah would later become the place where Solomon built the great temple.

David built the altar there and offered burnt offerings for sin and peace offerings for restored fellowship with God. When David prayed, the Lord answered by sending fire down from heaven onto the altar to burn up the sacrifice. This miraculous fire was God's visible sign that David's offering was fully accepted and His anger was gone.

The Lord ordered the angel of death to put his sword back into its sheath. The angel obeyed, bringing the destructive plague to an immediate halt. Because the sacrifice had been accepted, God's justice was satisfied and peace was restored to Israel.

Once David saw that the Lord had answered his prayers and accepted his sacrifices at Ornan's threshing floor, he continued to worship God there. He recognized that the Lord had chosen this specific hill as a holy place of meeting. From that day forward, it became an ongoing place of worship for the king.

The original sacred tent that Moses built in the wilderness, along with the bronze altar of sacrifice, was still located a few miles away at Gibeon. That was where the nation usually offered its public sacrifices. This historical detail explains why sacrificing at Ornan's threshing floor was unusual and needed God's special permission.

David could not travel to Gibeon to pray before the tabernacle because he was terrified by the angel's drawn sword. The danger to Jerusalem was far too urgent for a long trip, and he feared leaving the city unprotected while the judgment hung near. God met David where he was in his distress, showing that true worship can take place wherever the Lord reveals His presence.
